title: Model catalog story angles and sales hooks
content:
Goal
---
This is a working playbook of distinct narrative angles and quick sales hooks we can use to position the Model Catalog, Verified Profiles, and our model selection recommendations to technical and non-technical buyers. The aim: create modular messages that are short enough for sales outreach, expandable for product pages, and testable in landing pages and email sequences.

Status and context
---
Draft for GTM sync 2025-02. Pulling from recent benchmarks and customer discovery calls (Q4 2024 pilot accounts). Not final; intended to be split into email snippets, one-pagers, and side-by-side competitive bullets.

High-level messaging buckets (distinct story angles)
---
1) "Predictable economics, predictable outcomes" (Finance/Platform buyers)
- Core claim: Verified profiles reduce model selection risk and expected cost overruns by surfacing performance-by-workload and cost-per-1k-token estimates.
- Hook line (30s): "Choose models that match your SLAs and budget — our verified profiles show you the predicted latency, throughput, and unit cost for your workload so you don't learn the hard way in production." 
- Proof points: per-route latency charts, cost delta examples (gptx-large vs quantized Llama variant), customer quote from pilot: "Saved ~28% on token cost without latency regressions." 
- Objection handling: "We can run a quick 2-day eval on your traces and return a workload-fit card."

2) "Engineering-first risk controls" (Platform/Infra/Product)
- Core claim: Verified profiles include runtime-validated failure modes, memory/kv-cache characteristics, and fallback compatibility so infra teams can plan capacity and degrade gracefully.
- Hook: "Know how each model behaves under load and which variants will keep you within SLOs when traffic spikes." 
- Distinctiveness vs competitors: emphasize runtime telemetry (KV cache hit rates, batching behavior) rather than just model FLOPs or paper benchmarks. 
- Tactical play: ship an "SLO readiness" card in the console for each model with example autoscale configs.

3) "Product-first quality signals" (PMs, ML engineers)
- Core claim: Verified profiles tie model outputs to evaluative metrics (factuality, instruction-following, hallucination rate on our benchmarks) and show expected regression risk when swapping models.
- Hook: "Swap models without surprises — know which prompts and evaluation sets will change the behavior of your feature." 
- Experiment: provide a small eval suite for customers to run and auto-generate a delta report comparing two candidate models.

4) "Open models, curated and trusted" (Security/Legal/Procurement)
- Core claim: We make open models accessible but safe to adopt by certifying provenance, license compatibility, and known upstream changes.
- Hook: "Adopt open models with enterprise controls — audited footprints, license flags, and recommended guardrails included." 
- Messaging nuance: avoid moralizing open vs closed; emphasize practical controls (KMS, region pinning, data residency) and a clear remediation path when upstream models update.

Persona-specific quick scripts (30–60s)
---
A) Engineering lead (technical)
- Intro: "We built a model catalog that shows runtime-validated profiles — latency, kv-cache behavior, and memory headroom — so you can choose a model that fits your infra without trial-and-error."
- Enablement ask: demo the model-specific SLO card and a live throughput test from the console.

B) Product manager (outcome-focused)
- Intro: "We give you expected behavior deltas between models on your prompt set, plus suggested quant/embedding variants that preserve functionality while lowering costs." 
- Ask: Offer a free "delta eval" on two critical flows.

C) Procurement/Security
- Intro: "Each catalog entry includes license flags, provenance notes, and recommended guardrails — we surface whether a model has commercial restrictions and how to configure it safely."

Competitive analysis notes (concise, distinct bullets)
---
- Managed LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic): strength is single-source simplicity and brand trust. Weakness: limited visibility into runtime tradeoffs and unit-cost tuning. Our angle: deeper operational visibility + routing/fallback controls. 
- Cloud marketplaces (AWS Bedrock / GCP Vertex variants): strength is cloud-native integrations. Weakness: inconsistent model telemetry and often single-region constraints. Our angle: multi-deployment parity (hosted/dedicated/private) and workload fit cards. 
- Self-hosted runtimes (llama.cpp, private stacks): strength is cost/control. Weakness: heavy lift for production (autoscaling, latency SLOs, live fallbacks). Our angle: provide the production orchestration and verified performance profiles so teams don't re-build infra.

Positioning differentiator checklist (for marketing copy)
---
- "Verified" means runtime-validated on our serving runtime, not just a paper benchmark.
- Profiles include: latency percentiles, throughput at common batch sizes, memory/KV usage, cost-per-1k tokens estimate under typical batching, and eval metrics on our standard prompt suites.
- Include clear icons for: "SLO-friendly", "Low-cost variant available", "License audited", "Canary-ready".

Examples of short headlines and subheads to A/B test
---
- Headline A: "Pick models that actually run in production" | Subhead: "Profiles backed by runtime tests, cost estimates, and fallback plans." 
- Headline B: "Open models, trusted for production" | Subhead: "Proven performance, known failure modes, and enterprise controls." 
- Headline C: "Reduce model swap risk by 90%" | Subhead: "Compare behavior on your flows before you commit."

Objections we should pre-bake responses for sales
---
- "We already benchmark ourselves" → "We can ingest your traces and return an apples-to-apples workbook and a recommended default model config in 72h." 
- "Open models change frequently" → "Profiles include a provenance timeline and an alerting path; we can pin exact model artifacts and notify you on upstream releases." 
- "We need HIPAA/SOC2 controls" → "Private deployment and KMS integrations are supported; we'll scope a compliance plan."

Launch assets and experiments (short list)
---
- 1-pager: "How to read a verified profile" (visuals + example workload card)
- Interactive landing page: users upload a short prompt set (3–5 examples) and get a sample "fit card" (mocked) — run experiment with 2 CTAs: request demo vs try eval.
- Sales playbook: 3 outreach templates (cold, warm, technical deep-dive) mapped to persona. Track reply rate and demo conversion.

Metrics to monitor (for messaging efficacy)
---
- Landing conversion on interactive fit-card >= 6% (benchmark)
- Demo-scheduled rate after outreach >= 12% for technical leads
- Customer eval-to-purchase time reduction vs baseline (pilot cohort)
- Number of model swaps avoided or qualified as "bad fit" post-eval

Operational TODOs (near-term)
---

- [ ] Wire up a small demo pipeline that runs two models on 5 prompts and auto-produces a delta report. Owner: Ethan.
- [ ] Draft two email templates (short & technical) and A/B test. Owner: Priya.
- [ ] Prepare compliance blurb set (licenses, provenance) for security docs. Owner: Sofia.

Open questions / research asks
---
- What are typical batch size distributions for our top 10 hosted customers? (SRE/Telemetry)
- Which evaluation metrics resonate most with PMs vs SREs? (run interviews) 
- Is there a legal risk with providing explicit "cost-per-1k" estimates when underlying infra costs fluctuate? Need legal check.

Notes to self (informal)
---
- Keep the word "verified" narrowly defined: runtime-validated on Redwood serving runtime + known config. Avoid implying third-party cryptographic attestation. 
- Avoid heavy technical jargon in top-line pages; use it in the docs/playbook for technical audiences. 
- This doc should spawn: short sales snippets, a one-pager for procurement, an internal one-click eval job template, and a landing page A/B experiment.
